definition: Risk-as-feelings theory is the idea that people’s judgments about danger can be driven by rapid emotional impressions or intuitions, even when they have little objective information. In this context, perceived HIV risk reflects an immediate feeling-based sense of who seems safe or risky rather than an accurate assessment of actual risk.

reasons: The definition describes the theory broadly as driving “judgments about danger” by “rapid emotional impressions or intuitions”; the packet only supports reliance on “intuition” for identifying HIV risk and does not explicitly support “emotional impressions” or danger judgments beyond HIV risk.

The definition claims that “perceived HIV risk reflects an immediate feeling-based sense… rather than an accurate assessment of actual risk”; the packet supports that impressions of HIV risk can form “in a split second” and “despite a lack of information about the actual risk profile,” but it does not explicitly frame the basis as a “feeling-based sense” or contrast it in the exact terms used.

The definition generalizes to “who seems safe or risky”; the packet supports “judgments of HIV risk” and “first impressions,” including a “safeness” factor, but does not explicitly support the specific “who seems safe or risky” phrasing as the core mechanism.
The definition overgeneralizes beyond the packet, which is about first impressions of HIV risk; it does not support a broad claim about judgments about danger in general.

“Rapid emotional impressions” is not directly supported by the source; the packet supports intuition, split-second impressions, and judgments of HIV risk, but not a general emotional-process definition of the theory.
